files.lesson.md: --- order: 34 unit: algorithms10 node: AC9M10SP03 n2 uses: [AC9M10SP03 n1, AC9M9SP03 n2, AC9M8M06 n2] assumes: [AC9M10SP03 n1] connection: sprinkler-cover title: Write the algorithm summary: "Turn the pinned-down sprinkler job into numbered steps with a decision and a loop, exact enough for a machine, then run it by hand on two ovals." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Hand the sprinkler plan to a friend who has never seen the job. Could they follow it step by step and get your answer, with nobody to ask?" --- Last time you pinned the sprinkler job down: an oval that's L long and W wide, a spray that reaches r, and every point within r of a sprinkler. Now the plan has to be written so exactly that a machine could follow it. You found that one sprinkler covers a square a bit under 1.41 × r wide, so the plan uses 1.4 × r to stay on the safe side, and the oval is cut into cells that size or smaller with a sprinkler in the middle of each. The tricky part is deciding how many cells fit, so have a guess at that before the steps. ## Predict: how many cells? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a number of sprinklers shows who rounds a count down or to the nearest whole number. The algorithm's key detail is that a part-cell still needs a sprinkler, and the oval has two different sides to count." check: type: predict q: "One sprinkler covers a square about 11.2 m wide (made up). The junior oval is 40 m by 24 m. How many sprinklers does it need to be fully covered?" options: - "6 (3 across, 2 down)" - "8 (4 across, 2 down)" - "9 (3 across, 3 down)" - "12 (4 across, 3 down)" actual: "12. Across, 40 ÷ 11.2 is about 3.6, so a fourth sprinkler is needed for the last strip. Down, 24 ÷ 11.2 is about 2.1, so a third is needed even though the last strip is thin: 4 × 3 = 12." ``` You have a guess. Now here are the steps that give the answer. ## Run: the cell size ```step stage: run insight: "Following the first steps of the algorithm on a real oval shows that after rounding up the cells come out a little smaller than the biggest square, and that is why they stay covered." check: type: number q: "Steps 3 to 5 on the junior oval (L = 40, W = 24, r = 8): s = 1.4 × 8 = 11.2, then cols = 40 ÷ 11.2 rounded up. After that, w = 40 ÷ cols. How wide is one cell, in metres?" answer: 10 tolerance: 0 explain: "40 ÷ 11.2 ≈ 3.57, rounded up to 4 columns, and w = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m. The cell is narrower than 11.2 m, so its corners are covered." ``` ## Investigate: steps, decisions and loops ```step stage: investigate insight: "An algorithm for a spatial problem has computation steps, a decision that guards the input, and a loop that repeats one placement for every cell. Zoe's mistake is a wrong formula in the loop: the sprinkler goes on the cell's edge, not its middle." diagram: ref: diagrams.mmd#flow alt: "A flowchart of the sprinkler algorithm. Read the length, width and reach. A decision asks whether any of them is zero or less: if yes, say not an oval and stop. If no, set s to 1.4 times r, count the columns and rows rounding up, work out the cell size, place one sprinkler in each cell, then say the count and positions." caption: "The sprinkler algorithm" role: explain tasks: - check: type: sort q: "Here is the algorithm, step by step. What does each step do?" options: ["Computation", "Decision", "Loop", "Output"] items: - ["Step 2: If L, W or r is zero or less, say 'not an oval' and stop", "Decision"] - ["Step 3: Set s = 1.4 × r", "Computation"] - ["Step 4: Set cols = L ÷ s and rows = W ÷ s, each rounded up", "Computation"] - ["Step 5: Set w = L ÷ cols and h = W ÷ rows", "Computation"] - ["Step 6: For each row and each column, put a sprinkler in the middle of the cell", "Loop", "It repeats the same placing for every cell."] - ["Step 7: Say how many sprinklers, and where each one is", "Output"] explain: "A computation finds a number. A decision chooses between two paths. A loop repeats a step for every cell. The last step hands the answer back." - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Run the algorithm by hand on the senior oval: L = 60 m, W = 30 m, r = 8 m (made up). Write each step's result, then how many sprinklers it places." steps: - ["$s = 1.4 \\times 8 = 11.2$", "step 3"] - ["$\\text{cols} = 60 \\div 11.2 \\approx 5.36$, rounded up to $6$", "step 4: a part-cell still needs a sprinkler"] - ["$\\text{rows} = 30 \\div 11.2 \\approx 2.68$, rounded up to $3$", "step 4"] - ["$w = 60 \\div 6 = 10$ and $h = 30 \\div 3 = 10$", "step 5"] - ["$6 \\times 3 = 18$ sprinklers", "step 7: one in each cell"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why is 5.36 rounded up to 6, not down to 5?" options: - "Five cells would leave a strip at the end with no sprinkler" - "Six is always a better number than five" - "Rounding down would make the cells too small" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "It isn't about the number. Think about the last strip of the oval." - "Rounding down makes each cell bigger, not smaller, and then the corners are out of reach." answer: "18" answerLabel: "Sprinklers on the senior oval" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["15", "That's 5 × 3: the 5.36 was rounded down."] - ["12", "That's 6 × 2: the 2.68 was rounded down."] criteria: - "I used 11.2 for s and rounded each count up." - "I got the cell size from the rounded counts, not from s." - "I multiplied the columns by the rows." explain: "s = 11.2, cols = 6, rows = 3, cells 10 m by 10 m, so 6 × 3 = 18 sprinklers." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#zoe" text: "Zoe tries her algorithm on the junior oval (w = 10, h = 8) and finds the left end of the oval is out of reach of every sprinkler. Click the line where it goes wrong." answer: 6 fault: logic misconception: placement-at-cell-edge explain: "Line 6: x = i × w puts the first sprinkler at 10 m, the right-hand edge of its cell, so the cell's far corners are over 12 m away. The middle of the first cell is at x = 5, which is (i − 0.5) × w." smaller: check: type: number q: "On the junior oval each cell is 10 m wide. How far along the 40 m side is the middle of the first cell, in metres?" answer: 5 tolerance: 0 explain: "Half a cell is 5 m, so the middle of the first cell is at 5 m." - check: type: question q: "What is the loop in step 6 for?" options: - "To place a sprinkler in every cell without writing each position out" - "To check that the oval has a sensible size" - "To round the counts up" - "To stop the algorithm when the oval is covered" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "That's the decision in step 2." - "Rounding is a computation in step 4." - "The algorithm stops after the last cell by itself." explain: "The loop repeats one placing step for every row and column, so the same few words handle an oval with 12 cells or 120." ``` ```code diagrams.mmd#flow flowchart TD A[Read L, W and r] --> B{"Any of them zero or less?"} B -- yes --> C[Say not an oval, stop] B -- no --> D[Set s to 1.4 times r] D --> E[Count cols and rows, rounding up] E --> F[Work out the cell size] F --> G[Place a sprinkler in each cell] G --> H[Say the count and positions] class G new ``` ### Name each step Say which steps compute, which decide, and which repeat. Here are the steps in full. 1. Read the oval's length L, its width W and the spray's reach r, all in metres. 2. If L, W or r is zero or less, say "not an oval" and stop. 3. Set s = 1.4 × r. 4. Set cols = L ÷ s, rounded up, and rows = W ÷ s, rounded up. 5. Set w = L ÷ cols and h = W ÷ rows. 6. For each row j from 1 to rows, and each column i from 1 to cols, put a sprinkler at x = (i − 0.5) × w and y = (j − 0.5) × h. 7. Say how many sprinklers there are (cols × rows), and where each one is. ### Run it by hand Here is the whole algorithm run on the junior oval. ```worked s = 1.4 \times 8 = 11.2 :: Step 3. \text{cols} = 40 \div 11.2 \approx 3.57 \to 4 :: Step 4: round up, since a part-cell still needs a sprinkler. \text{rows} = 24 \div 11.2 \approx 2.14 \to 3 :: Step 4 again. w = 40 \div 4 = 10,\ h = 24 \div 3 = 8 :: Step 5. The cells come out a little smaller than the biggest square, so they stay covered. x = 5, 15, 25, 35;\ y = 4, 12, 20 :: Step 6: the middle of each cell is $(i - 0.5) \times w$ across and $(j - 0.5) \times h$ down. 4 \times 3 = 12 :: Step 7. ``` Now run it yourself on paper, on the senior oval, with the example beside you. Write each step's result, then pick the reason for rounding up. ### Find the mistake Check where Zoe's first sprinkler lands, and where its cell's middle is. ### What the loop does Think about what you'd have to write without a loop. ## Modify: change the oval ```step stage: modify insight: "Running the algorithm on an oval with an exact fit, on one that is just over, and with a different spray, to see what changes and what the algorithm does when the answer isn't the fewest." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Run it on an oval exactly 11.2 m long and 11.2 m wide (r = 8). How many sprinklers does it place?" answer: 1 tolerance: 0 explain: "11.2 ÷ 11.2 = 1 exactly, so cols = 1 and rows = 1. When the division comes out whole there's nothing to round up." - check: type: number q: "Run it on an oval 11.5 m long and 4 m wide (r = 8). How many sprinklers does it place?" answer: 2 tolerance: 0 explain: "11.5 ÷ 11.2 ≈ 1.03, which rounds up to 2 columns. 4 ÷ 11.2 rounds up to 1 row. So 2 × 1 = 2 sprinklers." - check: type: question q: "On that 11.5 m by 4 m oval, one sprinkler in the middle is only about 6.1 m from a corner, well inside 8 m. What does that tell you about the algorithm?" options: - "It always covers the oval, but it doesn't always use the fewest sprinklers" - "It left a dry spot, so it is wrong" - "It always uses the fewest sprinklers" - "It tells you nothing" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "Two sprinklers cover everything. The trouble is that one would have been enough." - "Here one would do and the algorithm placed two." - "It shows exactly when the algorithm gives more than it needs." explain: "The algorithm meets the 'must be true' rule, so every point is covered, but it doesn't meet the aim of using as few as possible when an oval is just over one cell." - check: type: question q: "The new sprinklers reach 5 m instead of 8 m. Which step of the algorithm has to be rewritten?" options: - "None: only the input r changes, and step 3 works out the new s" - "Step 3 only" - "Steps 3 and 4" - "All of the steps" answer: 0 feedback: - null - "Step 3 uses r, so it already adapts." - "Steps 3 and 4 use r through s, so they adapt too." - "The algorithm is written for any r." explain: "The steps use r rather than 8, so changing r changes every later number without rewriting a step." ``` ### An exact fit ### Just over one cell ### Enough, but not the fewest ### A different spray ## Practise: run it ```step stage: practise insight: "Running the algorithm on new ovals, finding a sprinkler's position, spotting a boundary case, and a review of a cell's half-diagonal." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Run the algorithm on an oval 50 m long and 20 m wide (r = 8, so s = 11.2). How many sprinklers does it place?" answer: 10 tolerance: 0 explain: "50 ÷ 11.2 ≈ 4.46 rounds up to 5 columns. 20 ÷ 11.2 ≈ 1.79 rounds up to 2 rows. 5 × 2 = 10." - check: type: number q: "On that oval each cell is 10 m wide. How far along the 50 m side is the middle of the first cell, in metres?" answer: 5 tolerance: 0 explain: "(1 − 0.5) × 10 = 5 m." - check: type: question q: "Which of these is a boundary case for the algorithm when s = 11.2?" options: ["An oval exactly 11.2 m long", "An oval 40 m by 24 m", "An oval 100 m by 50 m", "An oval 30 m by 20 m"] answer: 0 feedback: - null - "That's an ordinary case." - "That's an ordinary case, just a big one." - "That's an ordinary case." explain: "A boundary case sits right on the edge where the answer changes. At exactly 11.2 m the count is 1, and a hair over gives 2." - check: type: number q: "Review: a cell is 6 m wide and 8 m tall, with the sprinkler in the middle. How far is the sprinkler from a corner, in metres?" answer: 5 tolerance: 0 explain: "The corner is 3 m across and 4 m along from the middle: √(3² + 4²) = 5 m." ``` ### A new oval ### Where the first one goes ### A boundary case ### Review: corner to middle ## Make: the other oval ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the sprinkler job: running the whole algorithm on a new oval, then checking the answer against the success criterion." tasks: - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The caretaker's third oval is 36 m long and 20 m wide, with an 8 m spray (made up). Run the algorithm by hand. Write each step's result, then how many sprinklers it places." steps: - ["$s = 1.4 \\times 8 = 11.2$", "step 3"] - ["$\\text{cols} = 36 \\div 11.2 \\approx 3.21$, rounded up to $4$", "step 4"] - ["$\\text{rows} = 20 \\div 11.2 \\approx 1.79$, rounded up to $2$", "step 4"] - ["$w = 36 \\div 4 = 9$ and $h = 20 \\div 2 = 10$", "step 5"] - ["$4 \\times 2 = 8$ sprinklers", "step 7"] answer: "8" answerLabel: "Sprinklers on the third oval" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["6", "That's 3 × 2: 3.21 was rounded down."] - ["7", "Check the counts: 4 columns and 2 rows."] criteria: - "I rounded each count up." - "I found the cell size from the rounded counts." - "I finished with the number of sprinklers." explain: "s = 11.2, cols = 4, rows = 2, cells 9 m by 10 m, so 4 × 2 = 8 sprinklers." - check: type: number q: "Now test the answer. Each cell on that oval is 9 m by 10 m with its sprinkler in the middle. How far is the sprinkler from a corner of its cell, to 1 decimal place? Is it within 8 m?" answer: 6.7 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "The corner is 4.5 m across and 5 m along: √(4.5² + 5²) = √45.25 ≈ 6.7 m. That's within 8 m, so every point of the oval is covered." ``` ### Run it on the third oval Write this on paper first, a step at a time. ### Check the criterion **Also used in** - **Packing a van.** A loop places one box after another, a decision rejects a box that's too big, and the steps are exact enough for a program. - **Laying paving or tiles.** The same rounding up and the same cell by cell placing. - **Testing and refining.** The next job is to test an algorithm on awkward ovals, such as a curved one or one with a tree in the way, find where it fails, and improve it. That's for your class project. ```teacher summary: Students turn the pinned-down sprinkler job into numbered steps with a decision and a loop, run the steps by hand on two ovals, and find a bug where a sprinkler is placed on the edge of its cell instead of the middle (AC9M10SP03, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 17 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can write the steps of an algorithm exactly enough for a machine. - I can say which steps compute, which decide and which repeat. - I can run an algorithm by hand on two different inputs. struggle: "Rounding a count down, and putting a sprinkler on the edge of its cell. Ask: what is left over if you round down? Where is the middle of the first cell?" before: > Do the Predict and the senior oval yourself first. Students need Pin the problem down, Pythagoras and the Year 9 idea that an algorithm has computation and decision steps. The one idea: an algorithm is exact steps that work for any input. Here the steps cut the oval into cells no wider than 1.4 × the reach (the biggest square is about 1.41 × the reach, so 1.4 is on the safe side), with a sprinkler in the middle of each cell. A decision guards the input and a loop places one sprinkler in every cell. The steps always cover the oval, but they don't always use the fewest sprinklers: the 11.5 m by 4 m oval in Modify needs two when one would do. That is on purpose, to show the gap. Testing awkward ovals (a curved one, a tree in the middle), finding where the algorithm fails and refining it is node 3, the class project, and isn't covered here. The junior and senior ovals, the reach and the sizes are all made up. A flowchart or pseudocode both work; the numbered steps and the flowchart in the lesson say the same thing. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Most will say 6 or 9. Ask a student to say what happens to the leftover strip." - "Paper: the senior oval and the third oval are worked on paper first, a step at a time, with the steps beside you." - "Investigate: ask a student to point at the loop and say what would have to be written without it." - "Modify: before 11.5 m by 4 m, ask whether the algorithm will place one or two." - "Make: ask whether the answer meets the success criterion, and how they know." stuck: - see: A student rounds 3.57 to 4 for one side and 2.14 to 2 for the other. ask: What happens to the last strip on the short side? fix: "Round both counts up: any part-cell still needs a sprinkler." - see: A student sets the cell size to s, not to L ÷ cols. ask: Do the cells fill the oval exactly? fix: Divide each side by the rounded count, so the cells fit with no gaps. - see: A student puts the sprinkler at x = i × w. ask: Where is the middle of the first cell? fix: "Half a cell in: (i − 0.5) × w." stretch: Write the same algorithm in pseudocode with a loop that reads a list of ovals and prints each count, then try a staggered layout, where every second row is shifted half a cell, and see whether it needs fewer sprinklers. support: A printed copy of the seven steps and a blank table with columns for s, cols, rows, w, h and the count. leads: > This covers AC9M10SP03 node 2. Node 3 (testing, refining and justifying) is left to class: the project is to test this algorithm on the school's own oval, find where it fails, and refine it. Where it leads: the same habit of pinning down, then writing steps, then testing, for any spatial job. exit: q: A sprinkler reaches 8 m (s = 11.2). Run the algorithm on an oval 25 m long and 14 m wide. How many sprinklers does it place? a: 25 ÷ 11.2 ≈ 2.23 rounds up to 3 columns. 14 ÷ 11.2 = 1.25 rounds up to 2 rows. 3 × 2 = 6 sprinklers. explain: > An **algorithm** is exact steps that work for any input. Some steps compute a number, one decides whether to go on, and a loop repeats the placing for every cell. For the sprinklers: find s = 1.4 × r, count the columns and rows with each rounded up, work out the cell size, then put a sprinkler in the middle of every cell. It always covers the oval; it doesn't always use the fewest. ```

# Zoe's algorithm for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: zoe
Read the oval's length L, its width W and the spray's reach r.
Set s = 1.4 × r.
Set cols = L ÷ s, rounded up. Set rows = W ÷ s, rounded up.
Set w = L ÷ cols and h = W ÷ rows.
For each row j from 1 to rows and each column i from 1 to cols:
    put a sprinkler at x = i × w and y = j × h.
Say how many sprinklers, and where each one is.
# endregion
